questions.q: What is the key practical advantage of TD(0) over Monte Carlo methods?
options: TD(0) requires a known model of the environment
TD(0) can update its value estimates after every single step, without waiting for an episode to end
TD(0) always produces lower-variance estimates with zero bias
TD(0) only works for continuing tasks, never episodic ones
questions.explain: Unlike Monte Carlo, which must wait for the complete return at the end of an episode, TD(0) updates immediately after each transition using a one-step target.

questions.q: In the TD(0) update V(S_t) ← V(S_t) + α[R_{t+1} + γV(S_{t+1}) − V(S_t)], what is the 'TD target'?
questions.explain: The TD target, R_{t+1} + γV(S_{t+1}), is the one-step estimate of what V(S_t) should be, combining the real observed reward with the current estimate of the next state's value.

options: Because it requires restarting the environment after every episode
Because its update target uses the model's own current value estimate of the next state, rather than the actual complete return
Because it never uses a learning rate
Because it only works with tabular representations
questions.explain: TD(0)'s target leans on V(S_{t+1}), itself just an estimate, to update V(S_t) — using an estimate to improve another estimate, rather than waiting for ground truth like Monte Carlo's full return.

questions.q: Compared to Monte Carlo's target (the actual return G_t), how does TD(0)'s one-step target typically compare in terms of bias and variance?
options: TD(0) is unbiased with higher variance than Monte Carlo
TD(0) can be biased early in training (since it depends on an initially inaccurate V estimate) but typically has lower variance than Monte Carlo's full return
TD(0) and Monte Carlo have identical bias and variance properties
TD(0) has no bias and no variance
questions.explain: Because TD(0)'s target depends on only one sampled reward and transition (plus a current, possibly-inaccurate value estimate), it tends to have lower variance but can be biased while V is still inaccurate — unlike Monte Carlo's unbiased but higher-variance full-return target.
